screens.title: Preparing for XR Deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Before you hand your AR or VR app to users, there are deliberate steps that change a prototype into a deployable build. Today you will learn why installing the right Unity build modules matters, how to configure build and player settings for targets like Android and iOS, how XR Plug-in Management organizes AR and VR SDKs, and why signing plus a correct manifest keeps your app installable and functional. For example, enabling Android Build Support and the ARCore provider prevents missing-toolchain and missing-SDK errors that stop a build. This matters because build failures are often environmental, not code problems. You will also see concrete configuration values such as package names, minimum A P I levels, and recommended scripting backends. A common misconception is that Unity will automatically include every platform dependency; in practice you must enable modules and plugins deliberately to avoid bloated builds and runtime failures. By the end of this lesson you will have a checklist to switch platform targets, confirm Player Settings, enable XR providers, prepare signing credentials, and verify manifest entries. Think about the devices you want to target and which of these steps you should do first in your workflow.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Preparing for XR Deployment
Preparing for XR Deployment
An actionable orientation to the project-level steps that make AR and VR builds reliable.
In this lesson

Install build modules, configure Build and Player Settings, enable XR plug-ins, prepare signing keys, and verify manifest permissions so your XR app deploys cleanly.

Coming up

Step-by-step lab to add Android Build Support, switch platform, set Android Player Settings for ARCore, enable ARCore in XR Plug-in Management, and check the manifest.

Key takeaway

Deployment is configuration-heavy. Build modules, XR providers, signing, and manifest entries must be correct before building for a device.

Visual Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Project Prep Cards
Modules, Player Settings, XR Plug-ins, Signing
Recommended first step: confirm Unity has Android or iOS build modules installed through Unity Hub to avoid missing toolchain errors.
Keep keystore and passwords secure; losing them prevents app updates.
Explore Key Topics
Build Modules — Tools Unity needs to compile for each platform.
XR Plug-in Management — Enable ARCore, ARKit, or OpenXR per target platform.
Signing & Manifest — Digital identity and permissions required by stores and devices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this session you will be able to prepare a Unity project for XR deployment with confidence. First, you will recognize and install the necessary Unity build modules so your project can compile for each target device. Second, you will configure Build Settings and Player Settings to set package identifiers, A P I levels, scripting backends, and target architectures that match AR and VR platform requirements. Third, you will enable and manage XR providers through XR Plug-in Management so only the required SDKs are included. And fourth, you will prepare application signing credentials and inspect the application manifest to ensure required permissions like camera access are declared. Each objective pairs a specific configuration skill with a reason why it matters in practice, for example preventing build failures, avoiding store rejections, and protecting your ability to ship updates. As you learn, reflect on which target device you plan to support first and keep that device’s requirements in mind while adjusting settings.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Practical Objectives
Switch Active Build Target

screens.title: Unity Build Modules: Install and Verify
screens.narratorSegment: A primary cause of build failures is missing Unity build modules. These are optional components you select when installing Unity or add later through Unity Hub. They provide the compilers, SDK hooks, and toolchains Unity needs to create platform-specific packages. For example, Android Build Support bundles the Android SDK & NDK Tools and OpenJDK; without those, Unity cannot produce an APK or AAB. In practice, open Unity Hub, choose Installs, click the gear next to your Unity version, and select Add Modules to verify Android or iOS build support. After installing, confirm the external tools in Unity's Preferences show the Android SDK and NDK paths or let Unity manage them automatically. A common misconception is thinking the editor alone is sufficient; in reality, the editor plus correct modules is required. Example: a teammate on a different machine can open the same project but fail to build because their Unity install lacks Android Build Support. Checklists help: 1) Confirm Unity Hub module installed, 2) Verify SDK/NDK/OpenJDK paths in Preferences, 3) Restart Unity and attempt a simple Android build. Takeaway: installing modules early prevents wasted time later. What device will you target first?

keyIdea.title: Install build modules early
keyIdea.text: Add Android or iOS build support in Unity Hub and verify SDK/NDK/OpenJDK so builds can be produced on your machine.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Build Modules
Process: Add or verify modules
  1. Open Unity Hub → Installs → gear menu next to your version → Add Modules.
  2. Check Android Build Support or iOS Build Support, include SDK & NDK and OpenJDK where required.
  3. After install, open Unity Editor and confirm external tools via Edit → Preferences → External Tools.
  4. Restart Unity, then run a quick build to verify the toolchain.
Mnemonic: Hub, Modules, Preferences, Restart — follow these steps in order to reduce surprises later.
Common pitfalls and checks
Pitfall: Missing SDK causes "no toolchain" errors when building for Android. Check the SDK/NDK paths in Preferences.
Pitfall: Team members assume the project contains the build module. Each developer's Unity install must include modules they need.
Check: After module install, run an empty scene build to confirm a successful toolchain setup before adding XR features.
Example
Installing Android Build Support prevented a student from seeing compilation errors when exporting an ARCore APK. The missing OpenJDK had been the root cause.
Key Takeaway

Install and verify build modules early to avoid toolchain failures when building for your target platform.

screens.title: External Tools: SDK, NDK, and OpenJDK
screens.narratorSegment: When building for Android, Unity needs a collection of external tools: the Android SDK, the Android NDK, and the Java runtime toolchain, often provided as OpenJDK. The SDK contains platform libraries and build tools; the NDK provides native toolchains for compiling C and C++ code used by plugins and IL2CPP; OpenJDK supplies the Java tools required to sign and package Java-based parts of the build. Unity Hub can install these components alongside Android Build Support, but you should still confirm the paths under Edit, Preferences, External Tools. A common example is IL2CPP builds that fail because the NDK is missing; the error message might mention toolchain or clang. A common misconception is believing Android Studio alone satisfies Unity's needs; while Android Studio contains SDK tools, Unity needs the correct SDK/NDK versions and paths. In practice, verify the SDK, NDK, and JDK versions, let Unity manage them if possible, and run a test build. Takeaway: verify tool versions and let the editor point to correct paths to prevent cryptic native compile errors. Which build error would you check first when a test APK fails?

keyIdea.title: External tools explained
keyIdea.text: SDK, NDK, and OpenJDK are required for Android builds; verify installation and paths in Unity Preferences to prevent native compile problems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › External Tools
What each tool does
  • Android SDK: platform libraries and build utilities used to assemble APKs/AABs.
  • Android NDK: native compilers for C/C++ used by plugins and IL2CPP outputs.
  • OpenJDK: Java tools used during packaging and signing steps.
Verification steps
Open Edit → Preferences → External Tools. Confirm SDK and NDK paths or enable Unity's auto-managed options. Verify the OpenJDK checkbox if provided. After changes, restart Unity and run a small Android build to ensure all tools are functional.
Example: IL2CPP compilation failed with native error. The NDK was missing and installing the NDK via Unity Hub resolved the compile failure.
Common misconception

Assuming Android Studio installation alone fixes Unity builds. Unity requires compatible SDK/NDK versions and explicit paths or managed installs.

screens.title: Build Settings: Switch Platform and Scenes
screens.narratorSegment: Build Settings is where you declare a target platform, choose which scenes are included in the final package, and select build types such as Development or Release. Switching the active build target triggers asset re-imports because Unity may change platform-specific import settings for textures, shaders, or plugins. For a multi-platform project, switch platforms early to surface re-import issues before adding platform-specific code. As an example, select Android and click Switch Platform; expect the editor to re-import assets. Also, confirm the Scenes In Build list contains the scenes you want the app to start with. A common misconception is that all scenes in the project are automatically included; you must explicitly add the ones required. Another practical action is toggling Development Build to include debugging symbols when diagnosing startup or native plugin issues. Takeaway: switching platform and controlling scene inclusion are small, high-impact steps that should be part of your pre-deployment checklist. What scene will serve as your default entry point on devices? Build Settings: Switch Platform and Scenes means use build settings to set the active target and include the correct scenes to avoid asset re-import surprises and missing-scene builds.. In practical terms, select your target and define scenes for the build. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Build Settings
Steps to switch platform
  1. Open File → Build Settings.
  2. Select a platform such as Android and click Switch Platform.
  3. Wait for asset re-imports to complete and address any platform-specific warnings.
  4. Confirm Scenes In Build contains your startup scene(s).
Development Build is useful for debugging. Use Release builds for store submissions.
Visual checklist
Confirm: Active Platform shows Android (or iOS) after switch.
Confirm: Scenes in Build contains intended startup scenes; remove test scenes to reduce build size.
Watch: Asset re-import warnings may indicate incompatible plugins or shaders for the platform.
Key Takeaway

Switch platform early in development and manage your scene list to create predictable builds for your target device.

screens.title: Player Settings: Core Application Metadata
screens.narratorSegment: Player Settings contains the metadata and runtime choices that describe your application to the device and store. Company Name and Product Name form the base for package identifiers and bundle IDs. For Android, the Package Name is an identifier like com. yourcompany. yourapp; the example package com. cohortia. arplanedetector is a good template because it uses a reverse-domain style that stores expect. Version numbering matters for store updates and user visibility; increment version codes for each release. Another important choice is the scripting backend. IL2CPP is generally recommended because it converts managed code to native and tends to improve performance on many devices, but it affects build time and requires the NDK. A common misconception is that changing the product name alone alters the package identity; it does not. The package identifier governs whether the store treats a build as the same app. Takeaway: set consistent company, product, and package identifiers early and plan version increments to match your release process. Which package naming convention will you adopt for your app? Player Settings: Core Application Metadata means company, product name, package id, and version settings determine app identity and update behavior on stores and devices.. In practical terms, company, product name, package identifier, and versioning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Player Settings
Key fields to set
  • Company Name and Product Name — human-facing and used for defaults.
  • Package Name / Bundle ID — reverse-domain identifier required by platforms.
  • Version and Version Code — increment for each store update.
  • Scripting Backend — Mono or IL2CPP; IL2CPP recommended for performance.
Example package: com.cohortia.arplanedetector — follows reverse-domain style and avoids collisions on stores.
Architecture note
The package identifier is the unique key the operating system and stores use to link updates. Changing the product name does not change this identifier. Plan your identifier before publishing to avoid forcing users to install a new app for updates.
Tip: Use a consistent company domain and include app purpose in the package name to make identification easier.
Check: Before first release, record your keystore and package name in your project documentation.
Key Takeaway

Set stable package identifiers and plan version codes; these values control app identity and update paths on stores.

screens.title: Android Player Settings: API Levels, Backend, Architectures
screens.narratorSegment: On Android, several Player Settings directly affect compatibility with ARCore and device support. Minimum A P I Level sets the oldest Android version you will support; ARCore requires A P I level 24 or higher. Target A P I Level should be set to the highest installed to meet store policies and access recent platform features. The Scripting Backend controls how your managed code is translated; IL2CPP is often recommended for better runtime performance and compatibility with native XR SDKs, but it requires the NDK and longer build times. Target Architectures such as ARMv7 and ARM64 determine which C P U families your build supports; for ARCore and modern devices, include ARM64. A common misconception is enabling every architecture to be safe; that increases build size. Instead, choose the architectures that match your audience and store requirements. Example configuration used in the lab: Minimum A P I Level 24, Target A P I Level Automatic (highest installed), Scripting Backend IL2CPP, Target Architectures ARMv7 and ARM64. Takeaway: make explicit, deliberate choices about A P I levels, backend, and architectures to balance compatibility, performance, and build size. Which architecture set will you start with for your target audience?

keyIdea.title: Android build choices
keyIdea.text: Set min/target API levels, IL2CPP scripting backend, and appropriate architectures like ARM64 to meet ARCore and device expectations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Android Settings
Recommended configuration
Minimum API Level: Android 7.0 Nougat (API 24) or higher for ARCore compatibility.
Target API Level: Automatic (highest installed) to align with store requirements.
Scripting Backend: IL2CPP recommended for performance and native plugin compatibility.
Target Architectures: ARMv7 and ARM64 for broad device coverage; prefer ARM64 where possible.
Trade-offs and misconceptions
Including more architectures increases download size. Choose architectures that match your target devices.
IL2CPP reduces managed overhead but increases build time and requires the NDK; plan CI builds accordingly.
Setting an old Minimum API Level to support more devices may exclude newer AR features or break compatibility with XR providers.
Example

Project example: Minimum API 24, Target API Automatic, IL2CPP backend, ARMv7 and ARM64 selected — a balanced starting point for ARCore builds.

screens.title: XR Plug-in Management
screens.narratorSegment: XR Plug-in Management is Unity's modern system for enabling XR SDK providers by platform. Instead of older centralized XR settings, this interface separates providers under each platform tab. For Android, enable ARCore; for iOS, enable ARKit; for cross-platform runtime support, consider OpenXR where supported. Enabling the provider does not always automatically install the package; Unity may prompt you to add the corresponding XR Plugin package from the Package Manager. The benefit of XR Plug-in Management is twofold: it keeps your project from including unused SDK code, and it provides a clear place to manage multiple targets. A common misconception is that enabling a provider is sufficient without checking the plugin package installation; missing packages will cause runtime failures. Example: After switching Android as the active build target, open Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management and check ARCore under Android. If prompted, install the ARCore XR Plugin via the Package Manager. Takeaway: always confirm both the provider checkbox and the package installation. What XR provider will you enable first for your app? XR Plug-in Management means enable provider checkboxes per platform and confirm xr plugin packages are installed so runtime features work correctly.. In practical terms, enable the right xr providers for each target platform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › XR Plug-in Management
How it works
Open Edit → Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management. Each platform has a tab where you can check the providers you need. Unity will prompt to install corresponding packages if they are not present.
Example: Under the Android tab, check ARCore. Unity will ask to install the ARCore XR Plugin if it is missing. After install, ARCore will be available at runtime.
Checks and pitfalls
  • Ensure the plugin package is installed in Package Manager; the checkbox alone is not enough.
  • Only enable providers you will use to keep build size minimal.
  • When targeting multiple platforms, enable providers per-platform tabs, not globally.
Key Takeaway

Use XR Plug-in Management to enable and manage platform-specific XR providers and confirm package installation to avoid runtime failures.

screens.title: Application Signing: Keystore and iOS Profiles
screens.narratorSegment: Application signing proves who built the package and protects update integrity. On Android, every APK or AAB must be digitally signed with a keystore. Unity lets you create or import a keystore under Player Settings → Publishing Settings. Store the keystore file and its password securely because losing them prevents you from releasing updates to the same package. On iOS, signing is handled through Apple's developer tools and requires provisioning profiles and certificates managed via Xcode and the Apple Developer portal. Android signing steps
  1. Open Project Settings → Player → Publishing Settings (Android).
  2. Create or import a keystore and key, set and confirm passwords.

Tip: Use a secure team vault and document the keystore location and password in your release process documentation.
iOS signing overview
iOS requires certificates and provisioning profiles managed through the Apple Developer portal and Xcode. Unity hands the built Xcode project to Xcode for final signing steps and archive uploads to the App Store.
Common misconception

You cannot recover an Android app's update path if you lose the original keystore; regenerating a keystore creates a different identity.

screens.title: Application Manifest: Permissions and Features
screens.narratorSegment: The application manifest declares the permissions and hardware features your app needs at install time. For AR applications, the camera permission is essential and commonly expressed as android. permission. CAMERA. Location-based AR requires location permissions such as fine location. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Manifest & Permissions
Typical manifest entries
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" />

<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera.ar" android:required="true" />
Edit or place AndroidManifest.xml in Assets/Plugins/Android to control merged output.
Checks and common issues
  • Confirm the camera permission is declared; otherwise runtime camera access will be blocked.
  • Check for AR-specific features required by SDKs; missing features can disable AR functions on some devices.
  • Use the manifest merger report to understand how multiple manifests combine into the final APK.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Configure Project for Android ARCore
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through configuring an AR Foundation project for Android and ARCore. Begin by opening Unity Hub, selecting Installs, and adding Android Build Support if missing. Next, open your project and go to File → Build Settings. Select Android and click Switch Platform; accept that asset re-import may take time. Then open Edit → Project Settings → Player and under the Android tab set Company Name and Product Name, and set the Package Name to the reverse-domain style example com. cohortia. arplanedetector. Set Minimum A P I Level to 24 or higher, Target A P I Level to Automatic highest installed, select IL2CPP as the scripting backend, and choose ARMv7 plus ARM64 architectures. Now open Edit → Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management and enable ARCore under the Android tab. If Unity prompts to install the ARCore XR Plugin package, install it from the Package Manager. Finally, inspect Assets/Plugins/Android/AndroidManifest. xml and verify camera permission and the AR hardware feature entry. A common misconception is skipping the plugin installation step after checking the provider box; always verify the package. Takeaway: follow these steps in order to create a reliable ARCore build. screens.title: Troubleshooting Pre-deployment Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When a build fails or an XR feature doesn't behave, a systematic checklist helps you find the cause quickly. Start by confirming the build modules are present. If the error mentions missing toolchains, check the SDK, NDK, and JDK in Preferences. If the editor fails during platform switch, inspect console logs for re-import errors and incompatible plugins. For runtime tracking failures, confirm XR Plug-in Management has the provider enabled and that the plugin package is installed. If the app crashes on startup on device, inspect the device log for missing permissions or native library load failures, and verify the manifest contains CAMERA permission and any AR hardware feature entries. If the store rejects your build, check package identity, signing credentials, and target A P I Level. A common misconception is blaming code first; many XR deployment failures stem from configuration or missing platform packages. Example fix: install ARCore XR Plugin via Package Manager after enabling ARCore in XR Plug-in Management to resolve runtime initialization errors. Takeaway: follow a stepwise checklist — modules, tools, platform switch, XR provider, manifest, signing — until the cause is found. Which check will you perform first on a failing build?

Troubleshooting checklist
  1. Confirm Unity build modules are installed.

Diagnostic examples
Symptom: Build fails with native compile errors → Check NDK and IL2CPP settings.
Symptom: AR features not initializing → Check that the XR provider is enabled and the plugin package is installed.
Symptom: App installs but camera access is denied → Check AndroidManifest camera permission and runtime permission prompts.

Start with modules and tools, then progress through platform, XR providers, manifest, and signing to isolate build and runtime problems quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Before you hand your AR or VR app to users, there are deliberate steps that change a prototype into a deployable build. Today you will learn why installing the right Unity build modules matters, how to configure build and player settings for targets like Android and iOS, how XR Plug-in Management organizes AR and VR SDKs, and why signing plus a correct manifest keeps your app installable and functional. For example, enabling Android Build Support and the ARCore provider prevents missing-toolchain and missing-SDK errors that stop a build. This matters because build failures are often environmental, not code problems. You will also see concrete configuration values such as package names, minimum A P I levels, and recommended scripting backends. A common misconception is that Unity will automatically include every platform dependency; in practice you must enable modules and plugins deliberately to avoid bloated builds and runtime failures. By the end of this lesson you will have a checklist to switch platform targets, confirm Player Settings, enable XR providers, prepare signing credentials, and verify manifest entries. Think about the devices you want to target and which of these steps you should do first in your workflow.

By the end of this session you will be able to prepare a Unity project for XR deployment with confidence. First, you will recognize and install the necessary Unity build modules so your project can compile for each target device. Second, you will configure Build Settings and Player Settings to set package identifiers, A P I levels, scripting backends, and target architectures that match AR and VR platform requirements. Third, you will enable and manage XR providers through XR Plug-in Management so only the required SDKs are included. And fourth, you will prepare application signing credentials and inspect the application manifest to ensure required permissions like camera access are declared. Each objective pairs a specific configuration skill with a reason why it matters in practice, for example preventing build failures, avoiding store rejections, and protecting your ability to ship updates. As you learn, reflect on which target device you plan to support first and keep that device’s requirements in mind while adjusting settings.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification steps you will practice during the lab walkthrough. You will learn to switch the active build target in Build Settings and recognize when Unity starts re-importing assets after a platform change. You will also open Project Settings to tune Player Settings including package name, minimum and target A P I levels, and scripting backend selection. In addition, you will enable the ARCore provider in XR Plug-in Management for Android and confirm whether the ARCore XR Plugin package is installed. Finally, you will inspect or create an AndroidManifest. xml entry for permissions like camera access and the AR hardware feature. Each objective ties a configuration action to a real check: if you cannot build, check modules; if runtime tracking fails, check XR provider and manifest. A useful misconception to watch is assuming default settings are always adequate; many platforms require explicit A P I level, architecture, and plugin choices. These skills make deployment predictable and repeatable in a team setting.

A primary cause of build failures is missing Unity build modules. These are optional components you select when installing Unity or add later through Unity Hub. They provide the compilers, SDK hooks, and toolchains Unity needs to create platform-specific packages. For example, Android Build Support bundles the Android SDK & NDK Tools and OpenJDK; without those, Unity cannot produce an APK or AAB. In practice, open Unity Hub, choose Installs, click the gear next to your Unity version, and select Add Modules to verify Android or iOS build support. After installing, confirm the external tools in Unity's Preferences show the Android SDK and NDK paths or let Unity manage them automatically. A common misconception is thinking the editor alone is sufficient; in reality, the editor plus correct modules is required. Example: a teammate on a different machine can open the same project but fail to build because their Unity install lacks Android Build Support. Checklists help: 1) Confirm Unity Hub module installed, 2) Verify SDK/NDK/OpenJDK paths in Preferences, 3) Restart Unity and attempt a simple Android build. Takeaway: installing modules early prevents wasted time later. What device will you target first?

When building for Android, Unity needs a collection of external tools: the Android SDK, the Android NDK, and the Java runtime toolchain, often provided as OpenJDK. The SDK contains platform libraries and build tools; the NDK provides native toolchains for compiling C and C++ code used by plugins and IL2CPP; OpenJDK supplies the Java tools required to sign and package Java-based parts of the build. Unity Hub can install these components alongside Android Build Support, but you should still confirm the paths under Edit, Preferences, External Tools. A common example is IL2CPP builds that fail because the NDK is missing; the error message might mention toolchain or clang. A common misconception is believing Android Studio alone satisfies Unity's needs; while Android Studio contains SDK tools, Unity needs the correct SDK/NDK versions and paths. In practice, verify the SDK, NDK, and JDK versions, let Unity manage them if possible, and run a test build. Takeaway: verify tool versions and let the editor point to correct paths to prevent cryptic native compile errors. Which build error would you check first when a test APK fails?

Build Settings is where you declare a target platform, choose which scenes are included in the final package, and select build types such as Development or Release. Switching the active build target triggers asset re-imports because Unity may change platform-specific import settings for textures, shaders, or plugins. For a multi-platform project, switch platforms early to surface re-import issues before adding platform-specific code. As an example, select Android and click Switch Platform; expect the editor to re-import assets. Also, confirm the Scenes In Build list contains the scenes you want the app to start with. A common misconception is that all scenes in the project are automatically included; you must explicitly add the ones required. Another practical action is toggling Development Build to include debugging symbols when diagnosing startup or native plugin issues. Takeaway: switching platform and controlling scene inclusion are small, high-impact steps that should be part of your pre-deployment checklist. What scene will serve as your default entry point on devices? For Android, the Package Name is an identifier like com. yourcompany. yourapp; the example package com. cohortia. arplanedetector is a good template because it uses a reverse-domain style that stores expect. When a build fails or an XR feature doesn't behave, a systematic checklist helps you find the cause quickly. Start by confirming the build modules are present. If the error mentions missing toolchains, check the SDK, NDK, and JDK in Preferences. If the editor fails during platform switch, inspect console logs for re-import errors and incompatible plugins. For runtime tracking failures, confirm XR Plug-in Management has the provider enabled and that the plugin package is installed. If the app crashes on startup on device, inspect the device log for missing permissions or native library load failures, and verify the manifest contains CAMERA permission and any AR hardware feature entries. If the store rejects your build, check package identity, signing credentials, and target A P I Level. A common misconception is blaming code first; many XR deployment failures stem from configuration or missing platform packages. Let's recap the essential concepts you should keep in mind. First, Build Modules are required components you add through Unity Hub to enable compilation for Android or iOS. Second, Build Settings selects the active target and scenes to include; switching platform early avoids re-import surprises. Third, Player Settings define package identifiers, A P I levels, scripting backend, and architectures that determine compatibility and behavior. Fourth, XR Plug-in Management enables platform-specific XR providers like ARCore or ARKit and requires package installation. Fifth, Application Signing uses keystores on Android and provisioning profiles on iOS to verify publisher identity and enable updates. Sixth, the Application Manifest declares permissions and hardware features such as camera access which are required by AR experiences. A common reminder: always back up keystores and check manifests before building. These items form a practical checklist to prepare an XR project for deployment.
